I've been farming this land for 45 years. My father farmed before me. I know this soil — it's deep loam, drains well, but goes dry fast in May and June if the rains don't come. That's why I sank the well. With some of my children working in the city now, I manage most of the field myself with my wife and whoever is home. I can't afford to experiment. I do what I know works.

**On wheat:** I'll plant the whole 10.1 mu to winter wheat in October, same as always. I'll get seed from the village supply station — the improved variety they've been pushing for the past several years, Kenong 199 or similar. I don't trust myself to save seed at my age and with my eyesight. I'll do a rotary tillage pass after maize harvest to work in the stalks, then broadcast base fertilizer and drill the seed. I'll split my nitrogen — some as base, the rest I'll side-dress at jointing in March. I'll water four times: pre-sowing, overwintering, jointing, and heading. I've cut irrigation before when it got expensive and my yield dropped. Not worth it. Two pesticide passes: one herbicide in winter, one fungicide spray at heading for the rust and scab that's been coming through more often these past ten years.

**On maize:** Right after wheat harvest in June, I'll plant maize on the same ground — no time to waste, the season is short. I've used hybrid seed for decades now, the yields are simply better. I'll go with a popular local hybrid, probably Xianyu 335 or whatever the agroshop recommends that's proven in this county. I won't do deep tillage — no time and the soil is still loose from wheat. I'll spray herbicide within the first few days. One irrigation if July is dry, two if it's a hot year. One more pesticide pass mid-season for corn borer if I see the damage starting. I'll apply more nitrogen to maize than wheat — it needs it, and I've learned not to be stingy there.

I'm not changing much this year. Things have been stable. The children send money home, so I'm not desperate, but I'm not going to waste inputs either.
